Re analysis of diet protein study

The simulation study showed that a protein-identity distance goes blind when samples share no accessions, and that a TM-Vec ground metric does not. This report applies the same comparison to real data: 111 mouse faecal metaproteomes across eight dietary protein sources (Blakeley-Ruiz et al., ISME J 19(1) wraf048), quantified by spectral counting.

There is no weighted-UniFrac arm. The simulation could align 480 proteins from four families and give it a ground metric; here the universe is ~19,000 proteins from a whole gut community, mostly non-homologous, and there is no alignment to build a tree from.

Sys.setenv(KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK = "TRUE")
reticulate::use_python(Sys.which("python3"), required = TRUE)

library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(here)
library(MicrobiomeStat)
for (f in list.files("R", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)

path  <- here("data", "test_study")
NPERM <- 9999

Data

ps <- readRDS(file.path(path, "ps.rds"))   # built and validated in data_curation.Rmd
ps
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 30561 taxa and 111 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 111 samples by 9 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 30561 taxa by 8 taxonomic ranks ]
## refseq()      AAStringSet:      [ 30561 reference sequences ]

Rarefaction

floor_depth <- min(sample_sums(ps))    # rarefy to the shallowest sample, dropping none

ggplot(data.frame(depth = sort(sample_sums(ps))), aes(seq_along(depth), depth)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = floor_depth, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "sample, sorted by depth", y = "PSMs") + theme_bw()

The shallowest samples sit within a few percent of each other, so there is no isolated outlier to drop and the cutoff (dashed line) is simply the minimum depth, 5760 PSMs. Taking it from min() rather than hardcoding it is what keeps that sentence true: any fixed number above the minimum silently discards the samples below it.

psd <- rarefy_even_depth(ps, sample.size = floor_depth, rngseed = 1,
                         replace = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

# T0 has no protein source, so the diet term is undefined for it
psd <- prune_samples(sample_data(psd)$phase != "baseline", psd)
psd <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(psd) > 0, psd)
sample_data(psd)$diet <- factor(sample_data(psd)$diet)
sample_data(psd)$dose <- factor(sample_data(psd)$dose)
psd
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 19192 taxa and 99 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 99 samples by 9 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 19192 taxa by 8 taxonomic ranks ]
## refseq()      AAStringSet:      [ 19192 reference sequences ]

Rarefying before pruning matters: rarefaction subsamples the raw counts, so it has to see the raw counts.

# same baseline exclusion as psd, built straight off ps instead -- this is the
# unrarefied counterpart the Differential abundance section uses; see there for why
psu <- prune_samples(sample_data(ps)$phase != "baseline", ps)
psu <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(psu) > 0, psu)
sample_data(psu)$diet <- factor(sample_data(psu)$diet)
sample_data(psu)$dose <- factor(sample_data(psu)$dose)
psu
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 27346 taxa and 99 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 99 samples by 9 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 27346 taxa by 8 taxonomic ranks ]
## refseq()      AAStringSet:      [ 27346 reference sequences ]

Embedding

TM-Vec1, the ground metric chosen in docs/ground_metric_models.md: its head was trained to regress the TM-score of protein pairs, so cosine similarity between two vectors is a predicted TM-score. The large SWISS-MODEL head (default as of embed_proteins(), trained through 1000 residues) is used here rather than the 300-residue head, since most of this proteome’s abundance falls between the two. Sequences are still truncated at 1022 residues, ProtT5’s own encoder limit – the large head narrows how much of that range is extrapolation, it does not remove the ceiling. The result is cached, keyed by exact sequence and model, not just protein id – a stale vector from a re-curated sequence or a different model can’t be silently reused.

# cache = FALSE on purpose: this chunk's own code never changes, so knitr's
# chunk cache would not notice that `psd` changed upstream (e.g. a different
# rarefaction depth) and would silently replay a stale Z. The rds file below is
# the only cache, and it lives in data/ rather than in the knitr cache directory.
model_tag <- eval(formals(embed_proteins)$model)  # whichever model this chunk actually calls
cache <- file.path(path, "embeddings_tmvec1_large.rds")
cached <- if (file.exists(cache)) readRDS(cache) else list(Z = NULL, seq = character(0), model = character(0))

full_seq <- stats::setNames(as.character(refseq(psu)[taxa_names(psu)]), taxa_names(psu))

# keyed off psu (unrarefied, baseline already dropped), not psd -- covers every
# protein either count matrix below could need, rarefied or not, so a later change
# to rarefaction depth or the DA section never has to come back through this chunk
reusable <- intersect(taxa_names(psu), rownames(cached$Z))
reusable <- reusable[cached$seq[reusable] == full_seq[reusable] &
                      cached$model[reusable] == model_tag]
need  <- setdiff(taxa_names(psu), reusable)
Zall  <- cached$Z

if (length(need)) {
  s <- substr(full_seq[need], 1, 1022)
  s <- s[order(nchar(s))]                       # length-sorted: keeps batches tight
  # Save every 2000 proteins rather than once at the end. The full pass is about
  # an hour, so an interrupted render resumes from the last block instead of
  # starting over.
  for (i in split(seq_along(s), ceiling(seq_along(s) / 2000))) {
    new_Z <- embed_proteins(s[i], batch_size = 16)
    Zall  <- rbind(Zall[setdiff(rownames(Zall), rownames(new_Z)), , drop = FALSE], new_Z)
    cached$Z <- Zall
    cached$seq[rownames(new_Z)]   <- full_seq[rownames(new_Z)]
    cached$model[rownames(new_Z)] <- model_tag
    saveRDS(cached, cache)
  }
}
Z      <- Zall[taxa_names(psu), ]
cnt    <- t(as(otu_table(psd), "matrix"))   # samples in rows, RAREFIED -- distances/PCoA only
cnt_da <- t(as(otu_table(psu), "matrix"))   # samples in rows, UNRAREFIED -- differential abundance only

Truncating past 1022 residues rather than excluding those proteins is a bet that they are usually low-abundance. length_abundance_profile() is what that bet is checked against: for every possible length cutoff, what fraction of the protein catalog and what fraction of total abundance would fall on the far side of it. No fixed threshold decides “too much” here – a cutoff a little past a round number (1050 vs. 1000, say) can be read directly off the curves rather than guessed at.

length_abundance_profile(cnt, full_seq, max_length = 1022) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 1300, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey30")

At the 1022aa line (dashed), 5.3% of the catalog by count sits past it, but the abundance curve – consistently above the protein-count curve throughout – puts 13% of total abundance there instead, roughly 2.4x its share by count. Part of that is specific, identifiable large protein families in this proteome that are individually abundant regardless of length – S-layer proteins, a TonB-dependent transporter (SusC), multi-domain metabolic enzymes such as pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase – riding on top of what the protein-count curve alone would predict.

1022aa is where the encoder stops, not where trust should stop – a protein truncated to 1022 of its 1300 residues still gets an embedding built from 79% of its real sequence, and cosine similarity to another protein over that shared N-terminal region is a real, partial structural comparison, not noise. Past that, two things bound how much a truncated tail can cost:

  • The sample-level distance (weightedRep(), below) is abundance-weighted over thousands of proteins at once. A single sample’s diet signal does not hinge on any one protein’s embedding quality; the aggregate is robust to a small fraction of the catalog being a rougher approximation, which is exactly the shape both curves above show – concentrated well under 1300aa.
  • The bin-level analysis (rollupStructural(), below) is a per-bin risk, not a proteome-wide one. A truncated protein grouped with the wrong bin, based on partial N-terminal similarity, is an ordinary clustering error. It only becomes a real problem if that protein dominates a small, otherwise-uninformative bin’s annotation – and a bin whose interpretation rests on one long, truncated member’s annotation should not be trusted regardless of why that member’s embedding is uncertain. That is a limitation of the underlying protein language model’s context window, not of the clustering or the weighting this package does with whatever embedding it is given.

1300 (dotted line) is a reasonable place to draw that trust boundary on this dataset: past it, only 2.2% of the catalog and 6.1% of total abundance remain, and the argument above weakens as the untruncated fraction of a protein keeps shrinking.

Results

Bray-Curtis and Jaccard are both protein-identity distances – two proteins are either the same accession or maximally different – and differ only in whether abundance enters: Bray-Curtis weights by how much of each protein was detected, Jaccard only by whether it was detected at all.

# cnt built in the Embedding section above, reused here
md <- data.frame(sample_data(psd))

# Weighted UniFrac on a structure tree fitted to the TM-Vec ground metric.
# UPGMA (fastcluster, O(n^2)) rather than BIONJ: on these embeddings BIONJ fits
# the ground metric better (cophenetic r 0.85 vs 0.73 on a 3,000-protein sample)
# but is O(n^3), which at this protein count is hours for a single tree.
rep_unifrac <- function(counts, Z, distance = "cosine") {
  G <- tmDist(Z[colnames(counts), , drop = FALSE], distance = distance)
  on.exit(gc(verbose = FALSE), add = TRUE)   # the ground matrix is gigabytes here
  weightedRep(counts, G, method = "unifrac",
              tree = structureTree(G, method = "upgma"))
}

G_tm <- tmDist(Z[colnames(cnt), , drop = FALSE])
tree_tm <- structureTree(G_tm, method = "upgma")
tree_fidelity <- cor(as.vector(G_tm),
                     as.vector(as.dist(ape::cophenetic.phylo(tree_tm)[labels(G_tm), labels(G_tm)])))

D <- list(`Bray-Curtis` = phyloseq::distance(psd, method = "bray"),
          `Jaccard`     = vegdist(cnt, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE),
          `weightedRep` = weightedRep(cnt, G_tm, method = "unifrac", tree = tree_tm))

Amount of protein, sex and age stay in the model as covariates; only the diet term is reported. by = "terms" is sequential, so term order matters – the nuisance covariates go first and diet last, so diet’s reported \(R^2\) is the share left over after dose, sex and age, the more conservative reading rather than the one that hands diet whatever it and a covariate share. Permutations are blocked within mouse, since each mouse contributes several samples. sex is constant within a mouse, so it has no valid permutation distribution under that blocking — it absorbs variance rather than being tested.

diet_test <- function(dl, nperm = NPERM) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(dl), function(n) {
  set.seed(1)
  a <- adonis2(dl[[n]] ~ dose + sex + age_week + diet, data = md, by = "terms",
               permutations = permute::how(blocks = factor(md$subject), nperm = nperm))
  data.frame(distance = n, R2 = round(a["diet", "R2"], 3),
             F = round(a["diet", "F"], 2), p = a["diet", "Pr(>F)"])
}))
res <- diet_test(D)
r2  <- setNames(res$R2, res$distance)   # name-based lookup for the prose below
gt(res)
distance R2 F p
Bray-Curtis 0.253 8.65 1e-04
Jaccard 0.175 4.67 1e-04
weightedRep 0.294 10.19 1e-04
 
for (n in names(D)) {
  print(plot_ordination(psd, ordinate(psd, "PCoA", distance = D[[n]]), color = "diet") +
          stat_ellipse(type = "t", geom = "polygon", alpha = 0) +
          ggtitle(n) + theme_bw())
}

Diagnostics

A PERMANOVA \(p\) can come from groups differing in spread rather than in location, and the test cannot separate the two on its own. betadisper can – bias.adjust = TRUE corrects the known bias from diet groups having different sample sizes, and significance comes from a permutation test blocked within mouse, the same restriction the PERMANOVA above uses, rather than anova()’s assumption of independent observations.

gt(data.frame(
  distance     = names(D),
  betadisper_p = sapply(D, function(d) {
    bd <- betadisper(d, md$diet, bias.adjust = TRUE)
    pt <- permutest(bd, permutations = permute::how(blocks = factor(md$subject), nperm = NPERM))
    round(pt$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1], 4)
  }),
  row.names = NULL))
distance betadisper_p
Bray-Curtis 0.0003
Jaccard 0.0001
weightedRep 0.2893

Null controls

A significant weightedRep PERMANOVA is not by itself evidence that TM-Vec’s learned geometry contributed anything – the ground metric might only be re-expressing something much simpler about the sequences. Two baselines probe that, neither requiring a model: amino-acid composition (20-d, does this reduce to what proteins are made of) and log length (1-d, does this reduce to how long they are). Both are run through exactly the same distance as the TM-Vec arm, so only the ground metric differs.

aa <- strsplit("ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY", "")[[1]]
Z_comp <- t(vapply(strsplit(full_seq, ""), function(ch) {
  tabulate(match(ch, aa), length(aa)) / length(ch)
}, numeric(length(aa))))
dimnames(Z_comp) <- list(names(full_seq), aa)

Z_len <- matrix(log(nchar(full_seq)), dimnames = list(names(full_seq), "log_length"))

r2_comp <- diet_test(list(c = rep_unifrac(cnt, Z_comp)))$R2
# log length is one column: a magnitude with no direction, so cosine is undefined
r2_len  <- diet_test(list(l = rep_unifrac(cnt, Z_len, distance = "euclidean")))$R2

null_res <- rbind(
  data.frame(baseline = "amino-acid composition", R2 = r2_comp),
  data.frame(baseline = "log length", R2 = r2_len),
  data.frame(baseline = "TM-Vec1 (weightedRep, from the table above)", R2 = unname(r2["weightedRep"])))
rownames(null_res) <- NULL
gt(null_res)
baseline R2
amino-acid composition 0.272
log length 0.261
TM-Vec1 (weightedRep, from the table above) 0.294

TM-Vec’s diet \(R^2\) (0.294) clears the length-only baseline (0.261), so this is not simply a restatement of how long the detected proteins are.

It does not clear the amino-acid composition baseline: composition alone reaches 0.272 against TM-Vec’s 0.294 – +0.022, composition ahead. TM-Vec is not reading noise, and it is not just reading protein length, but on this test it does not demonstrably read more than what a 20-number amino-acid composition vector already reads. That matches the same pattern the fold-discrimination check in docs/ground_metric_models.md found at the protein-pair level (ESM-2 8M AUROC 0.766 against a composition baseline of 0.585, a comparable margin) – composition confound is not a hypothetical here, it is measured twice now, at two different levels of the pipeline. The honest reading is that this report’s significant weightedRep result and the structural bins built on it are consistent with structure carrying the diet signal, but do not on their own rule out amino-acid composition carrying it instead. Separating the two needs a test where structure and composition disagree, not one where both happen to move together, which is what this dataset offers.

What Bray-Curtis and Jaccard are actually using

All three distances find a highly significant diet effect and land in the same broad range, which the simulation would not have predicted. The reason is that these are cage-housed lab mice searched against one protein database: samples really do share the same accessions, and exact accession identity is something Bray-Curtis and Jaccard can read directly. Jaccard’s lower \(R^2\) against Bray-Curtis’s is the presence/absence penalty: it throws away how much of each shared protein was detected, keeping only whether it was detected at all.

The test is to take that away. Give every sample its own private accession for each protein it detected. Counts, sequences and abundances are all unchanged — only the labels differ — so no two samples share an accession any more.

nz  <- which(cnt > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
lab <- paste0("protein", seq_len(nrow(nz)))   # masked: one private label per (sample, protein) detection

cnt_s <- matrix(0L, nrow(cnt), length(lab), dimnames = list(rownames(cnt), lab))
cnt_s[cbind(nz[, "row"], seq_len(nrow(nz)))] <- cnt[nz]
Z_s <- Z[nz[, "col"], ]
rownames(Z_s) <- lab

c(accessions_before = ncol(cnt), accessions_after = ncol(cnt_s),
  max_samples_sharing_one = max(colSums(cnt_s > 0)))
##       accessions_before        accessions_after max_samples_sharing_one 
##                   19192                  125578                       1
# This is the one arm that cannot use the structure tree. Masking expands the
# table to one private accession per detection -- 208,177 columns -- and every
# ground-metric method (unifrac, ot, rbf_mmd) would need that matrix explicitly,
# which is ~347 TB. `mmd` reaches the same distance through a single matmul and
# never forms it. The invariance being demonstrated does not depend on which
# method is used: no embedding-based distance can read an accession label.
res_s <- diet_test(list(`Bray-Curtis` = vegdist(cnt_s / rowSums(cnt_s), "bray"),
                        `Jaccard`     = vegdist(cnt_s, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE),
                        `weightedRep` = weightedRep(cnt_s, Z_s, method = "mmd")))
gt(res_s)
distance R2 F p
Bray-Curtis 0.051 1.00 1e+00
Jaccard 0.051 1.00 1e+00
weightedRep 0.259 9.06 1e-04

Bray-Curtis and Jaccard both collapse to the exact null. Every pair is now maximally dissimilar, so each distance matrix is constant and cannot express any grouping: \(F = 1\), \(p = 1\), and \(R^2 = 5/98 = 0.051\), which is simply the diet term’s degrees of freedom over \(n-1\) — the share any 5-df term receives when there is nothing to explain. weightedRep() returns exactly what it returned above, because a protein’s embedding does not depend on what its accession is called and the abundance-weighted mean is therefore unchanged. This arm is computed with method = "mmd" rather than the structure tree used everywhere else, for the reason given in the chunk above – masking makes the ground matrix too large to form. The invariance is a property of the embedding, not of the method: a structure tree built on masked labels would be the same tree with the tips renamed, since the embeddings feeding it are identical.

So Bray-Curtis’s and Jaccard’s whole result here rests on samples sharing literal accessions. That is a fair assumption within one colony, one database and one assembly. It stops being fair across studies, colonies or assemblies, where the same function arrives under a different accession — which is the case the representation distance is built for.

Differential abundance

Unrarefied counts (cnt_da, from psu), not the rarefied cnt the sections above use. Rarefaction earns its keep for a sample-level distance – Bray-Curtis and weightedRep need every sample on the same footing, and subsampling is the standard way to buy that. A per-bin model doesn’t have the same need: LinDA fits its own bias-corrected centered-log-ratio transform per sample, which already absorbs each sample’s own depth, so throwing away real counts on top of that would trade statistical power for nothing (McMurdie & Holmes, PLoS Comp Biol 2014, arguing rarefaction is broadly the wrong tool for differential-abundance testing specifically, as opposed to beta-diversity). Unrarefied keeps 27346 proteins against 19192 rarefied.

PERMANOVA tests whether diet structures the community as a whole; it says nothing about which proteins carry that signal. Testing all 27346 proteins directly would mean that many near-independent tests on units that mostly aren’t independent – protein groups are frequently homologous (docs/method_notes.md §1), so a chunk of those “tests” are the same signal counted several times. rollupStructural() collapses proteins into bins where every member has predicted TM-score above a threshold to every other member; both the conventional TM-score same-fold boundary (0.5, Xu & Zhang 2010, used to pick the embedding model above) and a stricter cutoff (0.7, tighter and more homogeneous bins at the cost of more of them) are run below, as two independent passes over the same counts and embeddings – multiplicity is paid once per structural unit within each pass, not once per accession, but the two passes are not compared to each other statistically, only side by side.

roll_both <- rollupStructural_thresholds(cnt_da, Z, cluster_threshold = c(0.5, 0.7))

rollupStructural_thresholds() builds the pairwise TM-Vec distance matrix and its linkage tree once and cuts it at both heights, rather than paying that cost (the slow part; the cut itself is nearly free) twice over for two separate rollupStructural() calls.

t6 <- read.delim(file.path(path, "annotated", "ExtendedDataTable6AnnotatedMicrobialMetaproteomes.txt"),
                 skip = 2, quote = "\"", check.names = FALSE, colClasses = "character",
                 comment.char = "", fileEncoding = "latin1")
is_dark <- function(ids) {
  a <- setNames(t6[["Consensus annotation"]], t6[["Protein Identifier"]])[ids]
  g <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(psu), "matrix"))[ids, "Genus"]
  is.na(a) & is.na(g)
}

TM-score >= 0.5

roll_05 <- roll_both[["0.5"]]
c(proteins = ncol(cnt_da), bins = ncol(roll_05$counts))
## proteins     bins 
##    27346     1321

LinDA (Zhou et al., Genome Biology 2022) fits a linear model per bin on centered-log-ratio-transformed abundance and corrects the compositional bias a plain lm() on relative abundance would carry – the same reason weightedRep() works on abundance weights rather than raw proportions directly. Its formula interface takes a random effect for repeated sampling of the same mouse, the model-based counterpart to the permutation blocking adonis2 used above.

73 of 1321 bins here are nonzero in fewer than 3 of 99 samples, LinDA’s own stated bar for “virtually no statistical power” – prev.filter drops them before fitting rather than testing and ignoring them. The remaining sparse bins can still report a singular fit (their between-mouse variance estimated at zero), which lmer warns about but does not treat as an error.

fit_05 <- linda(t(roll_05$counts), md,
               formula = "~ diet + dose + sex + age_week + (1 | subject)",
               feature.dat.type = "count", prev.filter = 3 / nrow(roll_05$counts), verbose = FALSE)

As with the PERMANOVA table, only the diet term is reported: a joint Wald test on all five diet coefficients per bin, LinDA’s counterpart to adonis2’s by = "terms".

L <- matrix(0, nrow = 5, ncol = length(fit_05$variables) + 1)
for (i in 1:5) L[i, i + 1] <- 1   # intercept + the 5 diet dummy columns
wald_05 <- linda.wald.test(fit_05, L, model = "LMM", alpha = 0.05)
rownames(wald_05) <- rownames(fit_05$output[[1]])   # linda.wald.test drops them; reused below

gt(data.frame(bins_tested = nrow(wald_05), bins_diet_sig = sum(wald_05$reject),
              fraction_sig = round(mean(wald_05$reject), 3)))
bins_tested bins_diet_sig fraction_sig
1248 635 0.509

51% of bins reject at padj <= 0.05 – consistent with the PERMANOVA result above: diet is not a handful of marker proteins, it reorganizes abundance broadly across the structural repertoire. That joint test has no size to it, though – diet has five levels and no single number is “the” effect. A volcano plot needs one effect size per point, so the five diet-vs-Casein contrasts already inside fit_05 are shown separately: one panel per diet, log2 fold change against Casein on the x-axis, each point one bin, red where that specific contrast rejects at padj <= 0.05.

diet_vars_05 <- grep("^diet", fit_05$variables, value = TRUE)
volc_05 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(diet_vars_05, function(v) {
  o <- fit_05$output[[v]]
  data.frame(bin = rownames(o), diet = sub("^diet", "", v),
             log2FoldChange = o$log2FoldChange, pvalue = o$pvalue, reject = o$reject)
}))

ggplot(volc_05, aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(pvalue), color = reject)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ diet, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "firebrick"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change vs Casein", y = expression(-log[10](p))) + theme_bw()

top_05 <- volc_05[volc_05$reject, ]
top_05 <- top_05[which.max(abs(top_05$log2FoldChange)), ]

members_05 <- names(roll_05$bin)[roll_05$bin == top_05$bin]
ann_05 <- setNames(t6[["Consensus annotation"]], t6[["Protein Identifier"]])[members_05]
tx_05  <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(psu), "matrix"))[members_05, c("Genus", "Species")]

ann_calls_05 <- unique(na.omit(ann_05))
ann_desc_05  <- if (length(ann_calls_05) == 0) {
  "none of them"
} else if (length(ann_calls_05) == 1) {
  sprintf("%d of them, all the same call: *%s*", sum(!is.na(ann_05)), ann_calls_05)
} else {
  sprintf("%d of them: %s", sum(!is.na(ann_05)), paste0("*", ann_calls_05, "*", collapse = ", "))
}
ann_plausibility_05 <- if (length(ann_calls_05) &&
                           all(grepl("glyco|hydrolase|GH[0-9]", ann_calls_05, ignore.case = TRUE)) &&
                           identical(top_05$diet, "Yeast")) {
  " -- glycoside hydrolases are plausible machinery for a yeast-cell-wall-heavy diet,"
} else ""

The single largest shift, in either direction, is bin bin68 on Yeast: +9.0 log2 fold change against Casein at \(p=\) 6.3e-35. Its 31 members come from 9 different genera – proteins TM-Vec1 grouped as one predicted fold despite sharing no organism, the case an accession-identity distance cannot follow through a diet shift at all. Extended Data Table 6 annotates 15 of them: Mannosidase , Alpha-L-rhamnosidase, GH92 family glycosyl hydrolase though this is one bin’s annotation coverage, not a pathway enrichment test.

info_05 <- data.frame(
  Protein = members_05, Genus = tx_05$Genus, Species = tx_05$Species,
  `Annotation (Table 6)` = unname(ann_05),
  `Length (aa)` = Biostrings::width(refseq(psu)[members_05]),
  `Mean count, Casein` = round(colMeans(cnt_da[md$diet == "Casein", members_05, drop = FALSE]), 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
info_05[[paste0("Mean count, ", top_05$diet)]] <-

Every member sits at or near zero on Casein and climbs on Yeast, which is what the fold change states in raw counts – not an artifact of the log-ratio transform.

rollupStructural_thresholds()’s complete-linkage guarantee is that every pair inside a bin has predicted TM-score >= 0.5 to every other member, not just to a nearest neighbor – true here by construction, but a heatmap shows what it looks like: the full pairwise predicted TM-score matrix for bin bin68, same protein order as the table above.

Zb_05 <- Z[info_05$Protein, ]
S_05  <- 1 - as.matrix(proxy::dist(Zb_05, method = "cosine"))   # cosine == predicted TM-score
dimnames(S_05) <- list(info_05$Protein, info_05$Protein)           # kept protein-indexed, reused below

df_05 <- as.data.frame(as.table(S_05))
names(df_05) <- c("i", "j", "TM_hat")
df_05$i <- factor(df_05$i, levels = info_05$Protein, labels = seq_along(info_05$Protein))
df_05$j <- factor(df_05$j, levels = info_05$Protein, labels = seq_along(info_05$Protein))

ggplot(df_05, aes(i, j, fill = TM_hat)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0.5, 1), name = "predicted\nTM-score") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(x = "protein, table row above", y = "protein, table row above") +
  theme_minimal()

The floor is 0.523, comfortably above the 0.5 cutoff, and the diagonal is exactly 1 by construction (cos(z, z) = 1).

Same model as the 0.5 pass above, on a different (stricter, more numerous) set of bins.

1169 of 4368 bins here are nonzero in fewer than 3 of 99 samples – prev.filter drops them before fitting, same as above. A sparse bin is also where the truncated-embedding risk from the Embedding section actually bites: a wrongly-placed long protein is an ordinary clustering error almost everywhere, but a low-information bin it happens to dominate is a bin whose interpretation should not be trusted – not a defect in rollupStructural_thresholds(), a limit inherited from the encoder underneath it.

fit_07 <- linda(t(roll_07$counts), md,
               formula = "~ diet + dose + sex + age_week + (1 | subject)",
               feature.dat.type = "count", prev.filter = 3 / nrow(roll_07$counts), verbose = FALSE)
L <- matrix(0, nrow = 5, ncol = length(fit_07$variables) + 1)
for (i in 1:5) L[i, i + 1] <- 1
wald_07 <- linda.wald.test(fit_07, L, model = "LMM", alpha = 0.05)
rownames(wald_07) <- rownames(fit_07$output[[1]])

gt(data.frame(bins_tested = nrow(wald_07), bins_diet_sig = sum(wald_07$reject),
              fraction_sig = round(mean(wald_07$reject), 3)))

14 of the bin’s 17 members have neither a Genus call nor a Table 6 annotation – invisible to a lineage-based method and to a profile-based one, grouped here on structure alone. The 2 most abundant of them (rows 1 and 2 in the table above) illustrate what that buys: their nearest annotated relatives within the bin are two different proteins – AB21-1_Cage1_bin.62_00494 (a GH92 family glycosyl hydrolase, predicted TM-score 0.949) for BT_AB5-1_Cage1_bin.90_01179, and AB20-1_Cage1_bin.115_00504 (a GH92 family glycosyl hydrolase, predicted TM-score 0.93) for BT_AB5-1_Cage1_bin.90_01166. That is not a function call, just a specific, testable hypothesis where Table 6 offers none at all – exactly the gap a sequence-only annotation pipeline leaves open and a structural ground metric can speak to.

Proteins with neither a Genus call nor a Table 6 annotation are about as common among the proteins LinDA flagged as diet-associated (at either threshold) as they are everywhere else in the dataset – being biologically important here (large fold change, high significance) bought them no better odds of being annotated. A structural ground metric does not fix the annotation gap, but it does not inherit it either: rollupStructural_thresholds() places every protein in a bin whether or not it has a database hit, and a bin’s annotated members give its unannotated ones a specific, checkable neighbor instead of silence.

Conclusion

All three distances find dietary protein source highly significant, with diet \(R^2\) of 0.253 for Bray-Curtis, 0.175 for Jaccard, and 0.294 for the representation — the representation now reads more diet signal than Bray-Curtis, not just as much of it. The gain is real but not large, and the reason it exists at all is measurable: these samples share accessions, so protein identity, weighted or not, was already a good feature here.

Two more results separate the representation from the other two. Bray-Curtis fails the dispersion check while the representation passes, so part of the Bray-Curtis effect is diets differing in how variable they are rather than in where they sit. And once accession sharing is removed, both protein-identity distances drop to the null while the representation is untouched.

The honest reading is that the representation buys robustness and, here, a little power too. It keeps working where Bray-Curtis cannot — no shared accessions, no alignment, no tree, no annotation.

What that robustness is not, on this dataset, is demonstrated structural information specifically. The null controls above clear a random-projection null and a length-only baseline, but not amino-acid composition, which explains more diet variance (0.272) than the representation itself (0.294). Everything downstream that reads as “structural” – the PCoA separation, the rollupStructural_thresholds() bins, the glycan-degrading bins bin68 (TM-score >= 0.5) and bin66 (>= 0.7) – is equally consistent with TM-Vec’s geometry tracking amino-acid composition rather than fold. This report does not have the test that would separate those two explanations; that needs cases where composition and structure disagree, and this real metaproteome does not obviously supply enough of them.

What this report does not settle is alpha diversity. Rarefying equalises depth, not evenness, and any abundance-weighted set distance can respond to how concentrated a sample is as well as to what is in it. Separating the two needs evenness matching or a support-corrected estimator, neither of which is done here.
